title: How to design a robot arm with linkages
heading: How to design a robot arm with linkages, by describing it to AI
description: Design a desktop robot arm with all motors in the base, belts, push rods and parallelograms: AI lays it out, animates it, checks collisions and adds a gripper.
summary: A Dobot-style robot arm with three real NEMA 17 steppers in the base, laid out by SOMA AI from one description, animated with a collision check and given a parallel gripper.

video.title: How to Design a Robot Arm Without Any CAD Skills

chapters.label: Describe the arm in plain words
Range of motion and collision check
More reach, and a parallel gripper

answer: A robot arm with linkages keeps its motors in the base and drives the joints through belts and push rods, while parallelograms keep the tool mount level in every pose. Instead of working out link lengths, dead points and collisions by hand, you can describe the arm to SOMA AI, the agent built into SOMA: it lays out the linkage around your real motor, animates the full range of motion, checks every pose for parts that touch and narrows the joint limits where needed. The result is a first layout, not a tested robot: check torques, fits and loads before you build one.
need: SOMA, free and open source, for Windows, macOS or Linux.

A sign-in for SOMA AI: a ChatGPT Plus or Pro plan, or an API key from Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter or OpenCode. SOMA is free, the AI runs on your plan or key. The cheapest way to start is an OpenCode Go subscription for about $10 a month.
A STEP file of your motor, if you want the real one in the model. The video uses a NEMA 17 stepper from the FreeCAD Parts Library.
Your main numbers: the reach, the payload and how the parts will be made. The video uses about 250 mm reach, later 300 mm, a 200 g payload and 3D printed links.
Time: a full arm is a big job. In the video SOMA AI worked on its own for about an hour on each of the bigger steps.

steps.title: Import the motor as a STEP file
text: Start a new model. The video names it Robot arm.

The arm should get real motors, so first import a NEMA 17 stepper as a STEP file. It lands in the inputs folder. Click it in the file browser to see it in the viewer; Back to model returns to your model.

image.alt: SOMA's viewer showing the imported NEMA 17 stepper motor with its connector, and the note Viewing inputs/NEMA_17_with_connector.step, view only, with a Back to model button

steps.title: Describe the arm in plain words
text: Open the SOMA AI tab, pick the model and the effort. The video uses GPT-6.1 Sol with High effort, so it thinks longer before it acts.

Then describe the arm: what kind of arm it is, where the motors sit and which file to use for them, how the joints are driven, the reach and payload, how the parts are made, and which values you want to change later. Naming a known design such as a Dobot or uArm helps SOMA AI understand the layout you mean. End with a request to ask about anything that is unclear.
steps.prompt: Design a desktop robot arm like a Dobot or uArm. All motors sit in the base: one stepper turns the base, two more drive the shoulder and, through push rods, the elbow. Use the NEMA 17 from inputs/NEMA_17_with_connector.step for all three motors. A parallelogram keeps the gripper mount level in every pose. Reach about 250 mm, payload 200 g, 3D printed links, ball bearings and standard screws at the pivots. Make the base, shoulder and elbow angles parameters, and group the parts clearly in the structure tree. Ask me about anything that is unclear before you start.

steps.title: Answer its questions
text: SOMA AI asks its questions all at once, each with a recommended answer. In the video there were two: what the level wrist should carry, and how the two arm motors pass on their motion.
The video takes the recommendations: a mounting plate for your own gripper for now, and timing belts to gear down the two arm motors. Click an answer or write your own, then Send answers.

image.alt: SOMA AI has 2 questions: what the level wrist should carry, with Mounting plate only selected, and how the two arm motors transmit their motion, with Timing-belt reduction selected, above a Send answers button

steps.title: Let it lay out the linkage
text: Then SOMA AI works on its own, in the video for almost an hour. It lays out the links, the push rods and the belts, places the three motors, replaces screws that were too long, and checks the arm in ten poses for parts that touch. Every time it changes the model, SOMA builds it and shows it.

In the video the arm has 238 parts. The structure tree groups them from the fixed base and the rotating base up to the shoulder, the elbow drive, the leveling links and the wrist. Its summary lists 125 mm upper and forearm links, paired elbow push rods and two parallelograms that keep the mounting plate level.

image.alt: The robot arm with 238 parts next to its structure tree: Fixed base, Rotating base, Shoulder, Remote elbow, Leveling, Forearm, Level wrist and Pivot spacers, and SOMA AI's summary on the right

steps.title: Look at the motors inside
text: Make the two base groups see-through with the half circle next to their names, and the motors show: three copies of the imported NEMA 17.

In the video one sits under the turntable and turns the whole arm with a belt. The other two ride on the turntable, back to back, and drive the shoulder and the elbow through timing belts. From the side you see the linkage: paired push rods drive the elbow from the base.

image.alt: Close-up of the see-through base: a NEMA 17 stepper under the turntable, another stepper above it and a large belt pulley at the shoulder

steps.title: Animate the range of motion with a collision check
text: Does the linkage actually work? Ask for an animation of the full range of motion, with a collision check. SOMA AI writes the motion and checks every pose with the whole assembly, motors and screws included.

In the video that found contacts its first check had missed: the elbow axle touched the leveling links at steep angles, and screw heads hit the drive. So it moved the screws and narrowed the shoulder and elbow travel: shoulder 25 to 55 degrees, elbow 35 to 80 degrees. The base still turns ±150 degrees.
Open the Animation tab, pick the animation and press play. The push rods and the parallelograms follow, and the mounting plate stays level the whole time. The report: no collisions at 441 positions.
steps.prompt: Make an animation of the full range of motion: the base turns, then shoulder and elbow sweep to their limits while the gripper mount stays level. Check that no link hits another part, and limit the angles if needed.

image.alt: A frame of the animation: the arm with orange links and a level mounting plate, captioned Elbow sweep: 35 to 80 degrees, driven by the paired push rods

steps.title: Change it in words: more reach and a parallel gripper
text: Changes work the same way. Ask for more reach and a gripper whose jaws both move and stay parallel.

SOMA AI asked three questions first: where to measure the reach, which servo, and how wide the jaws should open. The video picks the reach to the center of the grip, a generic 9 gram servo for now, and 30 mm.

Then it worked for almost an hour: it lengthened the arm, built the gripper, extended the animation and checked everything again. The micro servo sits under the wrist plate and turns a small gear; two racks mesh with it from opposite sides, and each carries one jaw, so both jaws move the same distance in opposite directions. The collision check passed again, and so did the 14 builds at the ends of every parameter range.
steps.prompt: I need more reach: make it 300 mm, and add a simple gripper with a micro servo. Both jaws should move and stay parallel to each other while they open and close. Keep the animation working, and show the gripper opening and closing in it. Ask me about anything that is unclear before you start.

image.alt: Close-up from above of the first gripper: an orange gear between two orange racks, each joined to a jaw, and SOMA AI's summary of the 0 to 30 mm parallel gripper on the right

steps.title: Pose it with sliders
text: Because the prompt asked for it, the joint angles are parameters, and so are the reach and the jaw opening. You find them in the Parameters tab.

Drag a slider and SOMA rebuilds the arm in that pose, without the AI and without code: the push rods and the parallelograms follow, and the gripper stays level. Reset all brings the arm back to its home pose.

image.alt: The Parameters panel with Base angle, Shoulder elevation (shortened in the list), Elbow bend, Reach to grip center and Jaw opening; Shoulder elevation is set to 35 degrees and the Elbow bend slider is dragged to 45 degrees, 2 changed, next to the arm in that pose

steps.title: Redo the gripper from scratch
text: Look closely at what you got. In the video the first gripper opened and closed, but it was not usable: the jaws barely reached past the wrist, and every gripping force went through thin rods into the racks and the gear.

So start a new conversation and ask for a new gripper from scratch, with the jaws in their own guide that takes the forces. SOMA AI asked one thing first: the guide can take the bending and lifting loads, but something still has to hold the grip closed. The video picks the servo.

After 1 h 10 min of work there is a guide housing in which each jaw carriage runs on two T-shaped shoes, held in by a bolted lid. The fingers reach 48 mm beyond the housing, 40 mm further forward than before, and both jaws still move parallel, 0 to 30 mm. The racks are bolted on separately and, as chosen, still carry the closing force. To keep 300 mm of reach to the grip center, SOMA AI made the upper arm and the forearm shorter on its own.
steps.prompt: The gripper isn't usable yet. Please redo the complete gripper from scratch, don't keep the old geometry. The jaws should run in their own guide (a slide or rail housing) that takes all the gripping forces, so the racks and the gear only make the movement and never carry load. Also make the jaws reach further forward, so it can actually pick something up. Both jaws should still move parallel, driven by the servo.

image.alt: The arm with the new gripper: long orange fingers on a blue guide housing at the end of the linkage, and SOMA AI's summary after 1 h 10 min: independent captive slides, longer fingers 48 mm beyond the housing, parallel servo motion

tips: Import the real parts you want to use, like the motor, as STEP files first. Then the design is built around their true size.
Ask for the joint angles as parameters from the start. Then you can pose the arm with sliders and the animation can use the same angles.
Ask for a collision check of the whole assembly with every animation, and read the report. In the video it found contacts a simpler check had missed.
Look at the result with a critical eye. A gripper that opens and closes is not yet one that can hold something; say what is wrong and ask for a new one.
A new part adds weight. In the video the new gripper has about 136 g of printed parts, so little of the 200 g payload is left for the object. Test the real servo and the grip before you build.
For the best results the user guide recommends Opus 5.5 (with an API key) or GPT-6.2 Astra (with ChatGPT), with High effort or more.

faq.q: Why put all the motors of a robot arm in the base?
faq.a: Motors are heavy. When they sit in the base, the moving arm carries less weight, so it needs less torque, can move faster and bends less. The joints are then driven through belts, push rods or linkages. Desktop arms such as the Dobot and uArm use this layout.

faq.q: How does a parallelogram keep the gripper level?
faq.a: In a parallelogram linkage, opposite links always stay parallel to each other. If one side is fixed to the base and the opposite side carries the tool mount, the tool mount keeps the same angle while the arm moves. Two parallelograms in a row, one per arm segment, keep it level over the whole reach.

faq.q: Can AI check a robot arm for collisions?
faq.a: Yes, in SOMA. SOMA AI animates the arm through its full range of motion and checks the poses with the whole assembly, motors, bearings and screws included. In the video it checked 441 positions, found contacts, moved screws and narrowed the joint limits until nothing touched.

faq.q: How does a parallel gripper with one servo work?
faq.a: The servo turns a small gear. Two racks mesh with it from opposite sides, and each rack carries one jaw, so both jaws move the same distance in opposite directions and stay parallel. In the final version of the video the jaws run in a guide housing that takes the bending, lifting and twisting loads.

faq.q: Is an AI-designed robot arm ready to build?
faq.a: Treat it as a first layout. The geometry is exact and checked for collisions, but it is not a tested robot. In the video the servo is a placeholder; check the torques, the fits and the loads, and test the real servo and the grip before you print and assemble the parts.
